title: Paddy:
title_short: Paddy · My Dad Brought the Enemy Home
headline: The unsung heroes of the Irish peace were ordinary people, and it started at his own kitchen table.
story: Paddy grew up on the Irish border with a story that violence won independence. Yet his dad brought “the enemy” home to talk about peace. They argued. Then Paddy saw it: his dad was making safe spaces for people brave enough to tell their story.

At the International Fund for Ireland, nobody wanted them at first. But giving civic society a voice took the oxygen from the paramilitaries. The private peacebuilders are the unsung heroes, and they grow the next leaders. Warm, personal, hopeful.
do: Open on frame 1 on “my dad was bringing the enemy to our home” with the hook text.
Let the family story breathe. It is the way in.
Name super at 00:07, after the hook.
Stay on him for “the unsung heroes”.
Cover every trim with B-roll or a soft speech ramp.
dont: Do not use 00:30–00:36 (“everything that was bad was caused by the British … Protestants”).
Do not present his Israel / Palestine answer as advice. He says it “tends to have to be tailored”.
No camera-shutter sounds. No choppy jump cuts.

Auto-transcript of FX6_LVH_6405.MXF (Paddy, Brussels, 15 Sep 2026). Times are mm:ss in the source file. Speaker labels are often wrong: 00:55, 01:28, 02:48 and 05:47-06:05 are Paddy.
[00:02] Interviewer: Could you tell us about your work in Ireland, in Northern Ireland, and the most significant lesson you've learned?
[00:08] In the city of my background, my dad
[00:11] was a politician in Ireland who dedicated a lot of his life
[00:15] to peace building.
[00:17] I grew up in Ireland on the border
[00:21] with a narrative that said that our independence was achieved
[00:24] through a violent revolution.
[00:26] So violence was the premise of my narrative.
[00:30] And everything that was bad was caused by the British
[00:33] and, by extension, caused by Protestants.
[00:37] Yet my dad was bringing the enemy to our home
[00:40] to talk about peace and peace building.
[00:44] And I had very animated rows with him about this.
[00:49] But I eventually realized that what he was doing
[00:52] was creating safe spaces for people
[00:55] who were willing to take the risk to have their story told.
[00:59] And that's the lens through which I
[01:02] started to look at the world.
[01:04] And that world, in the 70s, was a very dark world.
[01:10] Nothing like the scale of Palestine and the Israeli
[01:13] people are experiencing.
[01:16] But on a day-to-day basis, it was quite dark.
[01:21] So I started to work with the International Fund for Ireland
[01:24] in the field in very challenging environments
[01:28] where no one wanted us.
[01:31] Republicans didn't want us, Irish Republicans,
[01:34] (reason given: not used)
[01:42] The unionist community didn't want us
[01:43] because we were United Ireland people.
[01:46] The British and Irish governments sat off.
[01:49] So it was a very innovative, groundbreaking approach
[01:57] by giving agency to civic society
[02:01] and enabling civic society to have the resources to say
[02:07] to government, we want to negotiate with you now.
[02:11] And it began to take the oxygen away from the paramilitaries.
[02:16] So the role that civic society has played in Northern Ireland
[02:21] are really the unsung heroes of the peace process,
[02:24] the ones you never hear about, the private peace builders.
[02:28] So my work is trying to make sure
[02:33] that everyday peacemakers get credit for the major role they
[02:38] played.
[02:40] And I'm pretty confident that the people who ended up
[02:45] at the negotiating table on the Good Friday agreement
[02:48] would not have been there had civic society not
[02:52] been confident enough to speak for itself.
[02:56] And they ultimately needed votes.
[02:58] So they ultimately went because civic society
[03:02] demanded that they go.
[03:12]-[04:11] (how the International Fund for Ireland is set up: not used)
[04:11] So it started to work in very fractured communities,
[04:15] communities that were under control of paramilitaries,
[04:18] work from the ground up, work with the community,
[04:21] build programs with the community,
[04:24] and trust that the communities with our support
[04:29] were going to deliver better things for where they lived.
[04:34] And that's quite crucial because the politicians
[04:40] can't touch things for all the obvious reasons.
[04:45] But civic society can, and it eventually nurtures leaders.
[04:53] You don't have to wait for your next John Hume, who
[04:55] was magnificent, Nelson Mandela, Gandhi.
[05:00] They emerge when you work closely with civic society,
[05:03] and that's what the International Fund did
[05:05] over 40 years on the 18th of September this year,
[05:10] this Friday.
[05:16] Interviewer: Could you speak about the applicability of that to the Israeli topic?
[05:25] It is always very difficult to transfer good practice
[05:31] from one situation to another.
[05:33] It tends to have to be tailored because if your value
[05:38] system is that you want to do things that the community needs
[05:42] most, then that's going to be very specific to the location.
[05:47] However, the rule, first of all, of working directly
[05:51] with communities and proactively working with communities,
[05:55] not waiting on open calls, proactively working
[05:58] with those in the most difficult of circumstances
[06:01] who have been disabled because of generally terrorist
[06:05] paramilitary activity.
[06:07] Working with them closely, you will always
[06:11] come up with things that are going to work.
[06:20] The single biggest grouping was focusing on young people.
[06:28] A, because they are the most vulnerable group of people
[06:31] to terrorists and paramilitaries.
[06:34] And if you don't protect them, then they
[06:36] will very likely end up there.
[06:40] Secondly, they're going to have to live in the world
[06:43] in the future as well as everyone else.
[06:46] But they're going to have to be part of it
[06:48] because it's going to be their world.
[06:52] You focus with youth in order to give them
[06:55] an alternative to being involved in violence and paramilitarism.
[06:59] So focusing on youth is one of the proudest things
[07:02] they ever did.
[07:03]-[08:48] (the youth internship programme and the Island of Ireland Peace Tower in Belgium: not used)
